entries.label: The grammar a town is generated by
entries.reason: Authored: a town is generated by the city grammar, the one grammar whose records state streets, premises and the walking surfaces a society walks and traffic drives.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: The version of that grammar
entries.reason: Measured: version 4 sets each stop line back from the crossing it approaches and keeps a parking lane against each kerb of the high street, which traffic derives its bays from. The traffic compiler refused every version 3 town measured (a left turn passes another approach's stop line), so only version 4 towns hold traffic.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Length of the town, west to east
entries.reason: Measured: whole 128 m tiles, two or three, because the terrain stage covers a town with whole tiles. Two tiles generated 60 of 60 towns at every block length offered, with 34 to 96 people. One tile at version 4 mostly does not generate (a kerb run too short for a crossing and the stop line before it), and four tiles held 132 to 242 people, more than a town's society ground admits. Three tiles need long blocks (the distance between cross streets says why), and with them the largest town this schema admits keeps its society's tick inside the tick budget the specification's bounds state.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Depth of the town, south to north
entries.reason: Measured: one tile deep. A town two tiles deep lays junctions where two local streets both run on through, and traffic refuses a junction whose every approach has priority: 23 of 23 such towns had their traffic refused, 14 for that reason.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Distance between cross streets

requires.reason: Measured: a town two tiles long needs cross streets at most 120 m apart. With 130 or 140 m its first cross street stands 63 or 58 m from the town's west edge, inside the 64 m margin a tile's document carries beyond its own edges, so the second tile carries the kerb that runs on past that street without the kerb it continues into, and the tessellator refuses that tile. Over every point this schema admitted before this rule, two towns at each (32 points, 144 tiles), the tessellator refused 16 tiles, every one of them this one, and baked every other. A later version of this schema lifts the rule once a tile carries the kerb that every kerb it carries continues into.

Measured: a town three tiles long needs cross streets at least 130 m apart. With 90 to 120 m most of its seed candidates held more people than its society ground admits or did not generate at all (with 120 m none of 10), and the towns that were kept held as many people as the ground admits on walking graphs of 1,100 to 1,180 places, where one tick took 154 ms at the median and 197 ms at the 95th percentile, at the edge of the tick budget; with 130 and 140 m, 24 of 24 towns tried were kept, on graphs of at most 906 places.

entries.reason: Measured: 90 to 140 m in 10 m steps. Two-tile towns generated at every length offered and their traffic compiled for 56 of 60. Three-tile towns with 130 or 140 m blocks generated 20 of 20 within the people bound; with 90 m blocks 5 of 10 fit it, with 100 or 110 m none of 19, and with 120 m none of 10 generated, so those are refused by name. Shorter blocks leave kerb runs too short for a crossing and a stop line; longer ones leave a two-tile town one block wide.

entries.label: Depth of a block
entries.reason: Measured: 56 m. With 60 m blocks no town one tile deep generated (0 of 120), because no street fits behind the high street; with 52 m blocks traffic compiled for 39 of 60 two-tile towns and with 56 m for 56 of 60; with 48 m a crossing often falls inside two junctions.

entries.label: Fewest storeys a building has
entries.reason: Measured: two or three storeys, the low end of a town's street wall. Bands of 2 to 4 and 3 to 5 storeys both generated every two-tile town tried; a band below its fewest is never offered, since the most storeys start at four.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Most storeys a building has
entries.reason: Measured: four or five storeys, a small town rather than a corridor of six-storey walls. Taller buildings hold more homes, and five storeys kept every two-tile town tried within the people one tick of its society was measured to hold.

entries.label: The side of the road traffic keeps to
entries.reason: Authored: the right, because the traffic simulation drives on the right only (docs/traffic-contract.md, its limits), and the grammar requires the side to be stated.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Rise and fall of the ground
entries.reason: Authored: level ground, because the terrain stage generates level ground only and walking surfaces stay within the step the city grammar publishes.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Width of a gutter
entries.reason: Authored: 300 mm, one width for the whole town, because the streets stage reads one gutter width along a whole street and refuses to derive it block by block.

entries.label: How far buildings stand back from the footway
entries.reason: Authored: none, so buildings stand on their frontage line and make the unbroken street edge of a town centre, as the small town and the corridor do.

licence.content_source: Authored for Exulanica world specifications; see the entry reasons

entries.label: Lots kept back as memory precincts
entries.reason: Authored: none, so every lot is built on and every building can hold homes and shops.
